newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - NatPower yr profits slip as tax looms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - NatPower yr profits slip as tax looms.

text.p: British electricity generator National Power Plc disappointed investors on Wednesday with a slip in year earnings and tried to defend itself against the new government's planned windfall tax on "excess profits".

"The company does not believe there is any evidence to show it has made excess profits...National Power does not believe it should be covered by the levy," chief executive Keith Henry said in a statement.
National Power said year pretax profits before exceptionals slipped eight percent to 740 million pounds ($1.2 billion) and it paid out a dividend of 25 pence, up from 23 pence.
Analysts had been expecting pretax profits between 760 and 792 million pounds and a dividend payout of 25-26 pence per share.
"The profits were a bit light...and the dividend increase was a bit thin," said Nigel Hawkins, analyst at Yamaichi.

Last year, National Power hiked its dividend 49 percent and iced the cake with a special dividend of one pound per share after it was blocked from buying a regional electricity company and told to sell some generating plant.
One analyst who asked not to be identified suggested that the single digit dividend growth this year reflected concerns over the proposed windfall tax.
"The market doesn't expect power generators to offer only single digit dividend growth. Maybe it's been shaved with an eye to the windfall tax," he said.
National Power shares were down 18.5 pence to 544 pence by 1010 GMT, reversing a strong performance recently which saw prices touch a 13-month high on May 16 of 582 pence.
Its fellow generator PowerGen, which reports annual results on Thursday, mirrored the losses with shares down 6.5 pence to 691 pence.

The new Labour government, which stormed to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has vowed to tax the "excess profits" of privatised utilities to finance a three billion pound programme to cut unemployment, but has yet to provide further details.
Analysts have suggested a total take of five billion pounds is likely, which could mean a potential payment by National Power and PowerGen of some 700 million pounds each.
Henry also claimed that the company was not regulated and faced competition, which should exclude it from any tax aimed at regulated monopolies.

In addition, he said taxpayers had already benefitted because during the period between sale of a first tranche of shares in 1991 and a final block in 1995, the government had retained 40 percent and had benefitted from dividends paid and the increase in the share price between the two dates.
The generator, which saw its market share slip to 24 percent in the UK last year from 32 percent previously, said it expected competition to intensify in the UK.
Over half of last year's market share slide was due to the sale of some plant, executives said, while the remainder was due to new plant coming onstream.
Finance director Roger Witcomb told an analysts' meeting that this year should see "a slight decline" in market share as the amount of new generation coming onstream this year would be less.
The company said in a statement with results that current trading was in line with expectations and added that earnings from overseas would continue to grow.
Over the longer term, it added, these earnings should "offset the forecast UK decline and...lead to resumed growth."
"National Power has reinforced its position as a leading international power business, in line with its long term strategy," chairman John Baker said in a statement with results.
The company now has equity investments of 900 million pounds overseas, chief executive Keith Henry said, with interests in areas such as Australia, Pakistan, U.S., Turkey and China.
But Hawkins said concern remained that "particularly on the UK...that the best is in the past."
The company said that it would consider "further limited reductions in dividend cover in the medium term, allowing continuing real dividend growth to be maintained."
Witcomb said this year's nine percent real dividend growth was "clearly an indication that we won't be going back to 49 percent increases and the (special) dividend that we gave last year."
But he added that "we have said in the past that for short periods we'd be prepared to go down as low as 1.5 (times)," for dividend cover, which is currently two times.
($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
